claims.claim_text: The economics that bound ASIC use are set by the fabs rather than by the devices: as processes move to tighter geometries on larger wafers the cost of a mask set rises, passing ten million dollars at the leading nodes, so an ASIC remains viable for an ever-shrinking set of applications.
claims.quote_verbatim: the cost of doing an ASIC continues to go up
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: The consequence is a volume threshold: the product has to ship in very high numbers before the mask set is recovered.
claims.quote_verbatim: So you have to have a very high volume of product to warrant doing it as an ASIC
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Volume is not the only justification. Absolute lowest power consumption and a range of other parametric requirements keep ASICs in use where the unit count alone would not.
claims.quote_verbatim: Or you want the absolute lowest power consumption or something like that
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: The break-even point has moved by orders of magnitude: around 1989 the dividing line was roughly a thousand pieces, and only in rare cases at that, whereas a thousand pieces today is nowhere near enough.
claims.quote_verbatim: we said the dividing line was around about 1,000 pieces
claims.speaker: Philip Frieden
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Philip Freidin - Xenodochial Xilinx Ex-Employee

claims.claim_text: Dedicated silicon wins on efficiency by a large factor rather than a small one: implementing a fixed function such as a turbo decoder as an ASIC rather than in an FPGA is worth something like twenty times, and possibly more. The obstacle is not the technology but that few organisations can afford to spin one.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're probably talking about 20x
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: The requirement that follows is that the application be both large and stable: the device has to be formed exactly to one application, and if that application is not huge the money is never recovered.
claims.quote_verbatim: So ASICs are always going to win. The problem is nobody can afford to spin them.
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Comparing the two on price alone is a mistake: area, physical size and, most critically, power consumption also separate an ASIC from a programmable part.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's not only about price. It's also about area and physical size and, most critically, power consumption as well.
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: The Cost Of Doing Business

claims.claim_text: A standard settling in a market removes the programmable option: once a video resolution and format are fixed, the volume manufacturers spin an ASIC for it.
claims.quote_verbatim: once a standard comes along, they spin an ASIC for it
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: The dividing line also moves because programmable parts grow: an FPGA in the 85,000 logic element class holds far more functionality than devices that were built as ASICs twenty years earlier.
claims.quote_verbatim: 20 years ago, they have been ASICs with far less functionality in there than the thing that we can build now with that FPGA
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: Open FPGA Toolchains at 35c3

claims.claim_text: For a purely digital design at an older process node there is little reason to make a chip at all — a microcontroller does the job. The distinctive case for a low-volume custom ASIC is analog and mixed signal: high-performance analog combined with a radio or a processor core on one die is something no other route produces.
claims.quote_verbatim: the analog and mixed signal is the, the, the unique selling points of a low volume custom ASICs
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: A niche is opening at low volume and high price per chip, where non-recurring engineering — the cost of the tools and of the team — dominates rather than the wafers, which is the case open-source tooling addresses.
claims.quote_verbatim: at that end of the market, your NREs dominate
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: The cost structure is almost entirely non-recurring: the first chip costs ten million dollars and the second costs ten million dollars and one dollar. That is what the volume question really asks.
claims.quote_verbatim: the first chip costs 10 million. The second chip costs 10 million and one, one dollar
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: The question of whether a system needs an ASIC is hard for the people who would benefit, because the knowledge of how an ASIC trades off against a two-chip or multi-chip solution sits on the ASIC side of the industry; the system designer dismisses the option on cost before evaluating it.
claims.quote_verbatim: The number one question is people will ask, do I need an ASIC?
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Those figures assume an advanced node and an outside design team. Bringing your own design effort to an older process can put the cost well below ten thousand dollars, for a chip that has what is needed and very little else.
claims.quote_verbatim: it could be well below $10,000
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Obsolescence is a distinct justification: an old board whose parts no longer exist can be re-implemented as a chip, weighed against a last-time buy of ten years of stock. The design files then belong to the owner, who can rebuild the part for as long as some fab will run it.
claims.quote_verbatim: The last thing actually is obsolescence mitigation
claims.speaker: Mohamed Kassem
claims.episode_title: Fabless Chip Design with Mohamed Kassem

claims.claim_text: Structured or metallised gate arrays sit between an FPGA and a full custom chip: the vendor has already fabricated an underlayer containing serialisers, memory blocks, multipliers and a sea of gates, and the customer buys only the metal layers that wire them together.
claims.quote_verbatim: the metalized gate arrays have an underlayer, which have different things like serializers on them and memory blocks and multipliers and just a sea of gates
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: The economics of that middle route are proportionate: the non-recurring cost is nowhere near the half-million dollars of a 65-nanometre mask set, and the price paid is a higher cost per part — perhaps four dollars where a full ASIC would have been one.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's not a half million dollars like a 65 nanometer mask set
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Target unit price is what drives the decision at the product level: the design in question needed the part under five dollars, against a twenty-dollar FPGA doing the same work.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're looking for less than $5 on the ASICs
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Moving a function from an FPGA into an ASIC is often driven by heat rather than by cost: an FPGA working hard on continuous data runs warm, and in a head-mounted product the thermal limit is the binding one.
claims.quote_verbatim: that FPGA is grinding pretty hard on all this data
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Chiplets apply the modular approach at silicon level: an existing die layout is reused and joined to others over a standardised interconnect, so a device can be assembled from off-the-shelf blocks and the design time cut.
claims.quote_verbatim: a chiplet is basically an, a preexisting IC layout
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Daaaamn We're Duuuummmb

claims.claim_text: Several competing interconnect standards exist — UCIe, which is serial and named by analogy with PCI Express, alongside Bunch of Wires and OpenHBI — with UCIe agreed among the major vendors and released in March 2022.
claims.quote_verbatim: this new chiplet interconnect standard
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Daaaamn We're Duuuummmb

claims.claim_text: One commercial expression of that model lets a customer select from a portfolio of chiplets in a browser and have the assembled device built for them, which makes the resulting part specific to that customer without a custom design effort.
claims.quote_verbatim: they would select from our portfolio of chiplets
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: The market for such a service is neither end of the spectrum: designers well served by existing microcontrollers and FPGAs do not need it, and organisations with effectively unlimited budgets already run thousand-person design centres. It is the middle — specialised requirements, real constraints on size, weight and power, and limited engineering budget, as in aerospace and defence.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's around a thousand person design center
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: The evaluation loop can be closed without silicon: selecting blocks emits the corresponding RTL, which is sent to cloud FPGA instances, loaded as bitstreams, and returned as a terminal session against the configured device within minutes.
claims.quote_verbatim: those designs get sent up to AWS to their FPGA instances
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Logic synthesis is the step that bridges a description to an architecture: the same adder written in HDL becomes a dedicated adder primitive, a chain of carry cells in an FPGA, or NAND and NOR gates for an ASIC, depending on what the target offers — the analogue of compiling a program to machine code.
claims.quote_verbatim: It might turn it into NAND gates and NOR gates for an ASIC synthesis task
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: Hardware description languages are among the genuinely portable standards: careful RTL that avoids vendor-specific IP blocks runs across different FPGA vendors' devices and can be taken into an ASIC without change, even though the languages are harder to work in than a modern software language.
claims.quote_verbatim: take the same Verilog code and, and use an ASIC without, you know, without changing anything
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: Accessible ASICs with Andreas Olofsson

claims.claim_text: Portability has to be designed for: inferring a memory by declaring an array in Verilog is hazardous because it binds the design to one vendor's primitives, so memories are wrapped behind a generic interface that can be re-implemented on a gate array, a full ASIC or another vendor's FPGA.
claims.quote_verbatim: You put a generic memory interface so you don't directly infer anything into your design
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Those wrappers must be explicit about polarity: an ASIC vendor supplied an I/O whose enable had the opposite polarity to the others, which nearly rendered a chip unusable and was recovered only in software.
claims.quote_verbatim: the ASIC vendor supplied an I.O. that had a different polarity enable than the other
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Prototyping on an FPGA transfers safely in proportion to how close the prototype is to the RTL that will be used in the ASIC.
claims.quote_verbatim: The closer you get it to the actual RTL that you're going to use in the ASIC, the safer it's going to be when you actually do the conversion
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: Because a respin is the only way to change fixed logic, flexibility is designed in deliberately: putting a small processor core on the die to handle low-level behaviour during idle periods means those functions are not hard-coded, and unused serialisers are left in place to be enabled if a later display needs them.
claims.quote_verbatim: we want to add as much flexibility as possible
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Absorptive Augmented Actuality

claims.claim_text: The nine-month wait for silicon shapes the whole development flow: after simulating the RTL against a test bench, the same design is ported to an FPGA with wrappers mapping the I/O to the device's pins, so the host microcontroller's firmware and the interface between them can be brought up and debugged long before the chip exists.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's going to take nine months for my ASIC to come back from the fab
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: Hardening is the last step and not a single one: throughout the process the design is repeatedly checked against whether it can actually be implemented — whether it meets the target frequency and fits the area — rather than only at the end.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're constantly making sure that your design can actually be implemented on the ASIC
claims.speaker: Julia Desmazes
claims.episode_title: Chip Design for Fun (and Waffles) with Julia Desmazes

claims.claim_text: ASIC place and route is not a clean compilation step: the design that comes out at the end typically carries a couple of thousand errors that have to be fixed by hand, in the way a board design rule check does.
claims.quote_verbatim: the design comes out and probably has, you know, a couple of thousand errors in the outputs that have to be fixed manually
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The conventional model is to prototype on an FPGA and then harden the whole design once, after which it stops changing. A more useful model would harden only the parts that have stopped evolving while the rest stays programmable — but FPGA vendors have no incentive to let a customer harden their PCI Express controller and stop buying their parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: you design on FPGA and then you harden your whole design into an ASIC and then you stop
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Most of the effort in building an ASIC is verification rather than design, because a tape-out cannot be corrected; the universal verification methodology is the established framework for it, and its System Verilog basis is the gap in open tooling.
claims.quote_verbatim: much of the work ends up being in the verification space
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Open Source Mindset with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Simulation is layered by cost: a behavioural simulator runs the known parts of the system fast, while the peripheral or block under development is simulated in HDL alongside it much more slowly, and because only part of the system is slow the overall result remains usable.
claims.quote_verbatim: most of the system is simulating very fast. And the part that you care about is simulated slower
claims.speaker: Michael Gielda
claims.episode_title: Simulating Embedded Hardware with Michael Gielda

claims.claim_text: Above simulation sits emulation in hardware: EDA vendors sell boxes containing grids of high-end FPGAs whose purpose is to run an ASIC design before it is committed.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have just these farms of FPGAs that are used to simulate in hardware, simulate ASIC designs
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Funding New/Manufacturing Old Projects - Radical Robotic Requisition

claims.claim_text: The specific failure that makes verification unavoidable is a state machine that can reach a state from which it cannot be unblocked, since there is no recovery short of a new mask at the cost of the original one — which is why formal methods are used where failure cannot be tolerated.
claims.quote_verbatim: we build a state machine into the ASIC that ends up getting stalled or blocked
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Stories from Supercon 2019

claims.claim_text: A chip cannot be bodged, so observability has to be designed in: internal sensors and current measurement in the support harness let a designer find out why something failed and improve it, rather than treating a tape-out as final.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's very hard to, uh, do bodge wires on an ASIC
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: Small teams can produce large chips because the work is at the level of top-level code: one company's chips were each done by fewer than three designers, and a 28-nanometre part of 200 million transistors was completed in twelve weeks by three engineers.
claims.quote_verbatim: the latest one we did at 28 nanometer is 200 million transistors that we did in 12 weeks with three engineers
claims.speaker: Andreas Olofsson
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Andreas Olofsson - Adapteva's Ampliative Abacus

claims.claim_text: Data does not flow in the ASIC industry because of how the agreements are structured: with several proprietary parties involved, obtaining the information needed for a design can require a three- or four-way non-disclosure agreement negotiated between organisations with different priorities and lawyers charging eight hundred dollars an hour.
claims.quote_verbatim: you need a three or four way NDA to get the data
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: The same agreements block reproducibility: research cannot be replicated if the raw data requires agreements with three separate companies to obtain, which suppresses the ability to demonstrate that one approach to a circuit is better than another.
claims.quote_verbatim: how do you reproduce, um, you know, somebody's research?
claims.speaker: Tim Ansell
claims.episode_title: Discussing the Open Source PDK with Tim Ansell

claims.claim_text: An open process design kit at 130 nanometres, with sponsored shuttle runs, made tape-out accessible on the condition that the submitted designs be open source.
claims.quote_verbatim: Google had sponsored a shuttle run through Skywater
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Chip Shortage Denier

claims.claim_text: A multi-project wafer slot is small but not trivial: roughly 3.3 by 2.8 millimetres, about ten square millimetres, which was enough to hold a set of a designer's FPGA-scale projects at once, and enough that nine separate designs shared one slot.
claims.quote_verbatim: you have about 3.3 millimeters by 2.8 millimeters
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: The mental model transferred from FPGAs misleads. An FPGA gives a flip-flop with every logic tile; an ASIC is a blank slate on which everything is placed, and a flip-flop turns out to be six to eight times larger than an inverter.
claims.quote_verbatim: you realize how much more huge a flip-flop is compared to an inverter
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: Bringing up a returned chip can require more instrumentation than the chip itself: one recovery used an FPGA to emulate the memory the on-die RISC-V core executed from, counted the instructions retired while sweeping the core voltage, and found an undervolted operating point at which enough instructions ran to configure the GPIOs.
claims.quote_verbatim: he made a really fancy system that used an FPGA to model the memory
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Open Source Tapeout with Matthew Venn

claims.claim_text: There is a graded path into the field: draw a few standard cells in a browser-based tool and run the automated flow to get a chip made; then build fundamental digital blocks — a full adder, a register, a linear feedback shift register — and test them; then learn a hardware description language.
claims.quote_verbatim: You could like draw a few standard cells in walkway, run it through the automated flow
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Component ranges on a die bear no relation to board level. Board designs use resistors from about one ohm to ten megohms and capacitors from a picofarad to ten thousand microfarads; on-chip capacitors run from femtofarads to picofarads.
claims.quote_verbatim: on ASIC, you're like fem to farads to pick a farads range
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: Absolute values on a die cannot be relied on: components can be matched to about one percent to each other on the same die but vary by around thirty percent from wafer to wafer, which is why analog design on silicon is done in ratios rather than absolute numbers.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll only be like 30% across wafers
claims.speaker: Matt Venn
claims.episode_title: Silicon Revolution with Matt Venn

claims.claim_text: The groups that benefit from cheap tape-out are small companies, universities and research institutions, and projects that would otherwise be stuck with an FPGA when what they need is a chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: projects that may normally be stuck with an FPGA and really need an ASIC
claims.speaker: Sam Zeloof
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Sam Zeloof

claims.claim_text: Access to processor IP has loosened under competitive pressure: the HDL for two ARM cores was put on the web for download under a licence that forbids using it in an actual ASIC, which reads as a response to RISC-V.
claims.quote_verbatim: recently ARM has put, uh, the code for the M0 and the M3 on their webpage
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Claire (née 'Clifford') Wolf

claims.claim_text: Bringing the signal chain into a custom chip is what enabled a low-cost instrument line to be designed and built in-house rather than rebadged: once the development is paid for, the chip itself costs a few dollars to produce, and it delivers performance the competition cannot reach.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you've put in the R&D funding to do that chip, you can churn out the chip like it's nothing
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Agilent, Analog, Cold Fusion - Funding Fusion Is Not Futile

claims.claim_text: That chip put the performance of an oscilloscope into a single device, and it was developed over several years by essentially one engineer.
claims.quote_verbatim: it pretty much comes down to one person
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Freescale, Hackerspaces, Printable Electronics - Publish Popular Parts Please!

claims.claim_text: Features are decided at chip design time and cannot be added later, which is why niche capabilities are excluded: independent time bases per input channel would have raised the complexity of the design substantially for a rare need, so the answer offered to a customer who needs it is a second instrument.
claims.quote_verbatim: we're not going to include it in the design of our ASIC chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: PCB Mills, SDR and Oscilloscopes - Flaunting Furbelow Fanciness

claims.claim_text: Dedicating one converter chip per channel removes a compromise built into shared designs: 6.25 gigasamples per second per channel that does not halve or quarter when further channels are enabled.
claims.quote_verbatim: So they've got an ASIC per channel
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Re-scoping the problem

claims.claim_text: Where a function is implemented decides whether it costs anything to use: with serial decoding, FFTs and measurements built into the chip, turning them on does not slow the instrument, whereas a single measurement left in software dropped the waveform update rate from a million per second to under a thousand.
claims.quote_verbatim: Somebody forgot to push that into the fabric
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Super Tecmo Bug

claims.claim_text: A custom front-end amplifier chip is amortised across an entire product line, appearing in the flagship and in models an order of magnitude cheaper, with the lower models deliberately limited in firmware.
claims.quote_verbatim: they use the same front end chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Pseudo Code...Pseudo Good

claims.claim_text: An ASIC can outlive the process that made it: when a fab retires a node the customer places a final order — perhaps a million parts — and ships product from that stock for years afterwards, which is why date codes on chips inside current instruments run years behind.
claims.quote_verbatim: we've still got a lot of stock of that chip
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Fan Fanboys

claims.claim_text: Eventually that runs out. A calculator ASIC designed in the 1980s could no longer be manufactured because nobody runs a 20-micron process any more, ending a product with a stable market.
claims.quote_verbatim: they couldn't actually make the ASIC anymore
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Biarchy Birthday Bavardage

claims.claim_text: Semi-custom parts are available to customers with sufficient volume: a large buyer can have an analog vendor spin a variant of an existing device. For everyone else, given time-to-market pressure, assembling the function from standard parts is faster than waiting for a perfect chip.
claims.quote_verbatim: they will actually design you a custom or semi-custom chip based on technology they already have
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Biarchy Birthday Bavardage

claims.claim_text: Very low-cost consumer instruments are built around a chip and almost nothing else: an epoxy blob with a few supporting passives is what makes a five-dollar multimeter possible.
claims.quote_verbatim: The way cheap Chinese volt meters work is they are all ASIC based
claims.speaker: Ian Danaher
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Daniher - Nascent Nonolith Numquid

claims.claim_text: The absence of a suitable part is itself a reason to make one: a design needing a DC-DC converter that would start at 0.6 volts found that no manufacturer made one, and had to spin its own chip because nothing on the market was close enough.
claims.quote_verbatim: they went, nobody has a chip for this
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Sipping Coulombs

claims.claim_text: A cryptographic mining algorithm is a good ASIC target precisely because it is simple: repeated bit operations that are easy to build in hardware and easy to run in parallel, which is where the advantage over a sequential processor comes from.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's just a very simple, very simple algorithm. It's easy to build in hardware.
claims.speaker: Ken Shirriff
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ken Shirriff

claims.claim_text: The same argument applies to inference: a fixed computation repeated over and over — object detection on a camera feed, say — is exactly what custom silicon is for, where an FPGA would cost more in silicon area, power and development time.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're just kind of making an inference engine, that's doing the same stuff over and over again
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Super Tecmo Bug

claims.claim_text: Converter performance in an instrument is bounded by clock jitter, which relates directly to the maximum effective number of bits achievable; the rapid improvement in instrument specifications came from 5 to 10 gigasample CMOS converters, where dense calibration algorithms can be built alongside the converter.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is a very simple equation that relates jitter of a clock of a converter to the maximum effective number of bits you can ever achieve
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: Above about 110 gigahertz the connector rather than the silicon becomes the limit: a one-millimetre connector is no longer 50 ohms at that frequency, so measurement moves to digitising in frequency bands or down-converting instead.
claims.quote_verbatim: At 110 gigahertz, your connector, one millimeter connector is no longer 50 ohms
claims.speaker: Shahriar Shahramian
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Shahriar from The Signal Path - Quisquous Quivering Quadripole

claims.claim_text: Decoy structures are placed on chips deliberately: circuits that do nothing, included so that someone x-raying the die spends months working out that they are not part of the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: they'll put in fake, fake circuits, basically
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Armstrong, Camenzind & Museums - Outstanding Oneirophoros Obituaries

claims.claim_text: Building a programmable device company requires three capabilities developed concurrently — the architecture, the software and the IC design — because working them sequentially yields a device two or three times larger than the best competing part. The software in question is the placement, routing and fitting algorithms, not the user interface.
claims.quote_verbatim: these three has to work concurrently cohesively to make the best products or technology
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Efinix FPGAs with Sammy Cheung

attribution_notes: eps 374, 392, 455, 498, 519, 650: attribution flagged unreliable. Claims are content-attributed to the guest whose company, chip or research the passage describes.

Speculation about market direction and host commentary on particular vendors' fortunes were dropped; what is kept is the economics that decide the make-or-buy question, the design and verification flow, and decision-relevant vendor history.
name: ASIC
